pitch.short: I spent six years inside Pinewick Paper & Print, a regional paper company, learning where its money and its paper went. The last three I spent on why cash sat in warehouses and where costs leaked. I build the model myself and walk the warehouse floor before anything goes into a deck.

about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls and studied business at Thornfield College of Commerce. In 2019 I joined Pinewick Paper & Print as an operations analyst, reporting to Gordon "Gordie" Pruitt, a regional manager who loved whiteboard acronyms. Pinewick taught me that every figure has an owner, and that the owner is usually in the warehouse. I became curious about what the figures said about the business: why wholesalers paid late, why one production line was dearer per tonne than the rest. Seven months on the finance team's cash taskforce in 2023 convinced me this should be my full-time work, and in 2025 I enrolled in the Whitlock School of Management MBA to move into consulting.
about.now: Co-editing the Consulting Club casebook, preparing for a 300 km ride this December, and singing with my teacher on Sunday mornings.

projects.title: Cash-cycle diagnostic for Pinewick's paper warehouses

working-capital.context: Pinewick makes paper reels, envelopes and packaging cartons at its Larchmont Falls mill and ships from Warehouse 3, with about $210M in revenue, roughly 70% sold to office-supply chains and corporate print buyers and 30% to independent wholesalers. Over three years the cash conversion cycle had stretched from 68 to 83 days, and the credit line was nearly full.
working-capital.problem: Gordon Pruitt believed the office-supply chains were paying late and had put the acronym on a whiteboard. Dennis Hale's taskforce had to explain the 15-day stretch and say which days could be won back within twelve months.
what_i_did: Extracted three years of receivables, stock and payables records from the ERP, then recomputed the cycle by month, channel and warehouse.
Showed that the chains paid on terms; independent wholesalers were at 79 days against 60-day terms, and that a single channel was behind 6 of the 15 days.
Reviewed the age of 1,800 slow-moving SKUs alongside the planning team, and walked Warehouse 3 with Wendell Odom to see what was really on the shelves.
Held three workshops with Dennis and the sales and supply heads, settling each lever with an owner and a number everyone could defend.
Produced the steering pack: a cycle bridge, eight levers ranked on cash and effort, and a plan for the first 90 days.

decisions.why: Contracts with the small local mills add 3% to the price if Pinewick pays after 45 days, so paying them later would cost more than the cash it freed.

decisions.choice: Count only stock we had seen
decisions.why: The ERP showed more slow stock than the warehouse held. Wendell remarked that a pallet nobody can find is a philosophical question, not an asset. We sized the stock lever only on what we counted; that shrank the figure and made Dennis readier to sign it.
It was the biggest lever that left production planning untouched, which meant Pinewick could start within a month.

results.note: worth 11 days of cycle time, spread over eight levers
two quarters after the taskforce, finance-reported

working-capital.learned: The ERP said one thing and the warehouse said another. Two days in Warehouse 3 moved the stock figure by a quarter, and that is why Dennis trusted the rest of the deck, rounding included.
working-capital.next: Tie wholesaler credit limits into sales bonuses, so the sales team, Marla Finch's included, shares the pain of late payment.

tile-pricing.context: The client is a mid-size stationery and notebook maker selling through about 360 independent retailers in two states. List prices went up 4–6% every year, while the average price actually realised per carton hardly changed.
tile-pricing.problem: Discounts leaked out at several points: printed on the invoice, paid back through quarterly schemes, granted as cash discounts, or absorbed as freight. No one saw the combined figure for one retailer, so two similar-sized retailers could end up paying quite different prices.
what_i_did: Prepared 29,000 FY26 invoice lines and scheme credit notes in Python, then matched them with freight bills.
Constructed a pocket-price waterfall for every retailer and product range, running from list price down to what the company retained after all discounts.
Plotted pocket price against retailer volume and found a spread of 3.8 points between similar-sized retailers.
Visited 12 retailers in Harlow Bay and Dunmere alongside the regional sales managers to learn how discount deals were struck.
Drew up volume-based discount bands, an exception approval matrix and a weekly leakage report, and ran them as a pilot lasting six weeks across two regions.

decisions.why: The sales team needed room to land big school orders. Anything outside the band went up to the regional head, so every exception stayed on view.
For far-away retailers, freight paid by the company came to 1.9 points of list price, and no discount report showed it.

results.note: pilot regions vs prior six weeks

tile-pricing.learned: The leakage came mostly from a handful of negotiating habits in each region. When regional managers saw their own retailers on the scatter chart, they began requesting the report weekly.
tile-pricing.next: Roll the bands out to the remaining three regions and merge quarterly schemes into them, so each retailer sees a single net price.
tile-pricing.my_role: Summer Associate, ran the pricing analysis and set up the pilot

cold-chain-entry.context: Pinewick runs one mill and three warehouses, all in Larchmont Falls. Its largest customers were asking for a depot closer to their own markets in neighbouring towns, and Gordon Pruitt had already drafted a motivational poster about expansion.
cold-chain-entry.problem: Pinewick could fund one new depot over the next year and a half and had to pick from Oakhaven, Briarwick, Stillwater Cross and Marrow Bend. Customers had asked for all four, yet nothing put them on a comparable footing.
what_i_did: Estimated demand in pallet positions for each product group (office paper, cartons, stationery, print-on-demand) for each town, from mill output figures, buyer consumption estimates and interviews.
Built a supply list of existing depots in each town from planning filings, haulier calls and site visits in two towns.
Interviewed 37 people: 15 wholesalers and print buyers, 9 depot operators, 7 haulage brokers and 6 of Pinewick's own customers.
Rated each town for demand shortfall and ease of entry (land prices, power hook-up, anchor customers) and put all four on a single chart.
Presented a phased plan to Gordon: Oakhaven first, Briarwick second, with the anchor customers signed before construction.

decisions.why: Most existing storage in these towns is old single-product shed space. Including it would have masked the shortfall in mixed paper and carton handling.
If two wholesalers took 40% of the space, year one would pay for itself, so anchor customers got the heaviest weight in the entry score.

results.note: willing to talk about taking 40% of a 6,000-pallet depot
three land parcels in Oakhaven shortlisted

cold-chain-entry.learned: My first top-down estimate put Briarwick on top. Then the haulier calls revealed two big depots due there in 2026, and the order flipped. Since then I give supply the same care as demand.
cold-chain-entry.next: Hand Pinewick a town-level model it can refresh yearly as capacity arrives, beginning with Briarwick.
